claims.text: The initial composite consists of discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
The initial W–Cu composite exhibits phase separation.
Interfacial voids in the untreated W–Cu composite compromise thermal conduction.
A high-pressure HIP annealing treatment will suppress phase separation in W–Cu.
A high-pressure HIP annealing treatment will eliminate interfacial void formation in W–Cu.
HIP at elevated temperature promotes solid-state diffusion and interfacial bonding in W–Cu.
HIP can form coherent, well-bonded, void-free W–Cu interfaces.
Improved W–Cu interfacial integrity creates a more continuous thermal-conduction pathway.
High-pressure annealing mechanically suppresses void nucleation at W–Cu interfaces.
Closing interfacial gaps reduces thermal barriers and improves overall heat conduction.
The conductivity benefit from HIP will persist in the presence of irradiation-induced microstructural stresses.
After identical thermal and irradiation exposure, HIP-treated W–Cu will have fewer interfacial voids and less phase separation than conventionally processed W–Cu.
After identical thermal and irradiation exposure, HIP-treated W–Cu will have higher thermal conductivity than conventionally processed W–Cu.
Interfacial voids and phase separation reduce the service reliability of untreated W–Cu joints.
The intervention is effective only when HIP temperature and pressure avoid excessive grain growth and deleterious reactions.
Service temperatures or irradiation fluxes beyond the designed regime may introduce other failure modes.
HPHT treatment has produced coherent interfaces in another alloy system.
HPHT-induced interfaces can relieve interfacial stress concentration and arrest interfacial cracking in another alloy system.
HPHT processing has been shown in other systems to reduce void-related defects.
